newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Bangladesh sign Ganges water-sharing pact.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh sign Ganges water-sharing pact.

text.p: India and Bangladesh on Thursday signed a landmark treaty to share water from the Ganges River, witnesses said.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina of Bangladesh signed the 30-year agreement on the last day of her three-day visit to the Indian capital.
The treaty removes the greatest irritant in relations between the two South Asian neighbours.

Bangladesh and a large section of northern India depend on water from the Ganges. The level of water can vary dramatically, flooding large areas during the monsoon months or falling to dangerously low levels during the January-June dry period.

In 1977, the two nations signed an agreement to let Bangladesh take a guaranteed minimum of 34,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs) between October and June every year. But the guarantee was dropped in a new six-year accord signed in 1982.

The decades-old water dispute worsened after India built the Farakka Barrage in 1974, restricting the flow of the Ganges, which irrigates a sprawling area of northern India before emptying into the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh.

A senior Indian Foreign Ministry official said that under the new treaty, if the water flow at the barrage near the two countries' border was below 70,000 cusecs, the nations would split the water evenly.
If the flow was between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, then Bangladesh would receive 35,000 cusecs, the official said. Above 75,000 cusecs, 40,000 cusecs would be guaranteed to India.

At the signing ceremony, Deve Gowda and Hasina were flanked by their foreign and water resources ministers. The communist chief minister of India's West Bengal state, Jyoti Basu, who played a key role in negotiating the treaty, was also present.
West Bengal state, which borders Bangladesh, and its capital Calcutta are heavily dependent on the Ganges.
At a banquet on Wednesday evening, Deve Gowda said the treaty opened a new chapter in bilateral relations.

"Let this agreement on the sharing of the Ganges waters be a stepping stone for greater cooperation between Bangladesh and India," Hasina said at the banquet. "We want to resolve this vexed issue once and for all."
Dhaka says India holds back water during the annual January-June dry season and releases excessive quantities during monsoon rains, causing flooding.
The agreement was expected to give a political boost to Hasina, who like Deve Gowda, assumed power in June following general elections.
Hasina's Awami League party regained power 21 years after her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, was assassinated in a bloody military coup.
Rahman became Bangladesh's first president after the Indian army fought a war with Pakistan that led to East Pakistan breaking away to become Bangladesh in 1971.

While water-sharing topped her agenda, Hasina was also believed to have discussed the future of a 25-year-old friendship treaty her father signed in March 1972. The accord has been criticised as a compromise to India by Hasina's rivals.

Hasina's party said before elections this year there was no need to renew the 1972 accord because the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), including both India and Pakistan, served the same purpose.
